pages.summary: The number of dimensions (always 2 or more).
body: Every array has at least two dimensions: a scalar and a vector are 1-by-1 and 1-by-n matrices. Trailing dimensions of length 1 are not counted beyond the second, so a 3-by-4-by-1 array has two.

Each looks only at the size: a scalar is 1-by-1; a vector is 1-by-n or n-by-1 (a scalar is both a row and a column); a matrix has two dimensions, whatever their lengths; a square matrix has as many rows as columns. Useful to check the inputs of a function.
syntax: True for a 1-by-n or n-by-1 array.
True for an array of two dimensions.

pages.summary: Remove the dimensions of length 1 (beyond the first two).
body: A slice taken along the third dimension of an array keeps its singleton dimensions: `A(2, 3, :)` is 1-by-1-by-n. `squeeze` takes them away; a matrix or vector is returned as it is.

examples.title: A slice through the pages of an array

pages.summary: Rearrange the dimensions of an array, and undo it.
body: `permute(A, order)` makes dimension `order(k)` of `A` the k-th dimension of the result: for a matrix, `permute(A, [2 1])` is the transpose. `ipermute` with the same order gives `A` back.
syntax: The dimensions of `A` in the order given.
The inverse of `permute` with that order.

examples.title: Pages become columns

pages.summary: Shift the dimensions of an array.
body: With `n` positive the first `n` dimensions move to the end (circularly); with `n` negative, `-n` dimensions of length 1 come first. Without `n`, leading dimensions of length 1 are taken away, and their number is the second output: a row vector becomes a column.
syntax: Leading singleton dimensions taken away, and how many.

examples.title: Shifting, and taking away leading singletons

pages.summary: Shift elements around in a circle.
body: The elements move `k` places along a dimension, those pushed off one end coming in at the other. A positive `k` shifts down (or right), a negative one up (or left). A vector of shifts moves along several dimensions at once.
syntax: Shifted `k` places along the first dimension that is not 1.

examples.title: The rows and columns of a matrix

pages.summary: Reverse the order of elements along a dimension.
body: `flip(A)` reverses a vector, or the rows of a matrix; `flip(A, dim)` reverses along any dimension. `fliplr` reverses the columns (left to right) and `flipud` the rows (up to down).
syntax: Along the first dimension that is not 1.

pages.summary: Turn a matrix by multiples of 90 degrees, anticlockwise.
body: `rot90(A)` turns the matrix a quarter turn anticlockwise: the last column becomes the first row. `k` quarter turns, negative for clockwise.

pages.summary: The lower or upper triangle of a matrix, the rest set to zero.
body: `tril` keeps the elements on and below the main diagonal, `triu` those on and above it. `k` moves the boundary: positive above the main diagonal, negative below.

pages.summary: The Kronecker product: every element of A times the whole of B.
body: The result is made of blocks `A(i, j)*B`, laid out as `A`'s elements are: an m-by-n `A` and a p-by-q `B` give an mp-by-nq matrix.

examples.title: Blocks of B, scaled by A

pages.summary: Matrix products and transposes of each page of an array.
body: An array of three or more dimensions is a stack of matrices, its pages. `pagemtimes(X, Y)` multiplies each page of `X` by the matching page of `Y` (a page of size 1 in a dimension is used against all of the other's), and can transpose either side first. `pagetranspose` and `pagectranspose` turn each page.

examples.title: A rotation matrix for each angle, applied to one point

pages.summary: Products of A and B summed over dimensions of each.
body: Contracts dimension `dimA` of `A` with dimension `dimB` of `B` (lengths must agree): the result has `A`'s other dimensions followed by `B`'s. Matrix multiplication is the contraction of `A`'s second dimension with `B`'s first. With no dimensions it is the outer product, and with `'all'` the sum of all of `A.*B`.
syntax: The sum of every product of matching elements.

examples.title: Matrix multiplication, and the inner product of two matrices

pages.summary: Linear indices from subscripts, and subscripts from linear indices.
body: The elements of an array can be named by their subscripts (row, column, …) or by one linear index counting down the columns. `sub2ind` turns subscripts into linear indices for an array of size `sz`; `ind2sub` goes the other way.
syntax: The linear indices of the elements at (`row`, `col`).
The rows and columns of linear indices.

examples.title: Both ways in a 3-by-4 matrix
Where a maximum is

pages.summary: The number of nonzero elements, and the nonzero elements themselves.
body: `nnz` counts the elements that are not zero; for logical arrays it counts the true ones, which makes it a quick count of how many elements pass a test. `nonzeros` gives the nonzero values as a column, in column order.
syntax: The nonzero elements, as a column.
